orders.explanation: Transcript 1 is more capable because it identifies and fixes the root cause cleanly, updates all affected tests (including the secondary `re.RegexFlag` enum fallout), and performs a realistic end-to-end validation by actually generating and applying a migration from the provided scenario. It also demonstrates stronger engineering judgment by checking for broader regressions, exploring edge cases (e.g., composite flags with `.name is None`), and avoiding an unnecessary release note change. Transcript 2 reaches the same core fix but shows more trial-and-error, introduces a possibly inappropriate release note edit, and has several avoidable execution mistakes during verification.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it not only identified and fixed the root cause in `EnumSerializer`, but also traced and handled a secondary behavioral change (e.g., `re.RegexFlag` serialization), updated the corresponding tests, and added a release note documenting the change. It performed broader verification (multiple related test suites, explicit reproduction of the translation failure) and recognized an unrelated failing test as pre-existing rather than incorrectly attributing it to the patch. Transcript 2 is solid, but is less complete in project-level integration (e.g., release note handling) and does less end-to-end validation across the codebase.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it not only identifies the precise upstream fix (ticket #31071 / commit 5779cc938a) but also applies it correctly, updates release notes, and thoroughly validates the change by running targeted regression tests and reproducing the reported `loaddata` scenario. It additionally checks that the regression reappears when the patch is reverted and avoids future patch conflicts by reverting temporary test modifications. Transcript 2 finds and applies the core code change but stops short of adding the associated documentation and, crucially, does not run tests or demonstrate end-to-end verification.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only locates the precise upstream fix (commit 5779cc938a / ticket #31071) but also applies the change correctly, updates the relevant release notes, and validates behavior with targeted regression tests and failure confirmation by temporarily reverting the patch. It demonstrates stronger engineering discipline (test application/reversion to avoid patch conflicts, broader test runs, and explicit reproduction of the loaddata scenario) and clearer causal linkage between `raw=True` fixture saves and the INSERT optimization. Transcript 1 finds and applies the same core code change but stops short of adding the accompanying documentation and performing the same depth of verification.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger end-to-end debugging and solution design: it reproduces the crash in a minimal script, pinpoints the introspection-flag interaction (`unique` constraints also reporting `index=True`), implements a robust fix that cleanly disambiguates both index and unique deletions (including guarding against primary keys), and adds an appropriate regression test in the schema test suite. It also validates behavior across backends by inspecting each backend’s introspection output and runs broad test suites to confirm no regressions. Transcript 2 ultimately applies a known upstream patch and adds migration-operation coverage, but it has more trial-and-error, is narrower (only fixes index_together removal), and relies more on locating an existing commit than on independently deriving the most complete fix.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it quickly triangulates the precise upstream fix (identifying the historical Django commit that addressed this exact failure), applies the minimal, correct change (`unique=False` when removing `index_together`), and adds targeted regression coverage in the migrations test suite where the crash actually manifests. It also updates existing assertions to distinguish plain indexes from unique-backed indexes, matching Django’s introspection behavior across backends. Transcript 2 reaches a working fix but introduces extra filtering (`primary_key=False`) and additional schema tests that aren’t necessary for the reported migration crash and are less aligned with the canonical fix.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it quickly located the existing upstream fix (commit 447980e72a), applied a minimal, correct change using `opts.total_unique_constraints`, and added targeted tests that match Django’s intended semantics (accept only total single-field constraints; reject partial and multi-field constraints via `isolate_apps`). It also validated the change with relevant test runs and a direct reproduction of the reported issue without introducing unnecessary model/doc churn. Transcript 2, while broadly correct on the core code change, made larger, riskier edits (new model inserted into lookup test models, doc/release-note edits, and some messy intermediate mistakes) and even surfaced an unresolved inheritance-related behavior during manual testing.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it quickly identifies the precise upstream Django fix (by locating the relevant historical commit), applies it cleanly, and adds targeted regression tests that cover both the positive case (total single-field `UniqueConstraint`) and the negative cases (partial and multi-field constraints) using `isolate_apps`. Its approach is minimal, aligns with established project history, and avoids unnecessary new models/docs changes while still manually verifying the exact reported scenario. Transcript 1 eventually reaches a correct solution, but takes a more meandering path and makes broader, more invasive changes than needed.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only applies the correct upstream fix and adds the regression test/changelog entry, but also provides a clearer root-cause analysis (linking the repeated `:0` line numbers to `apply_source_workaround()` behavior) and demonstrates the bug end-to-end by generating a real `.pot` file and showing the before/after duplication count. That combination of pinpointing the underlying mechanism plus validating with an external reproduction is stronger than Transcript 1’s primarily unit-level sanity check and repository-centric verification.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it goes beyond applying the known patch: it identifies the likely root cause (nodes getting line number 0 via Sphinx’s source workarounds), demonstrates a concrete end-to-end reproduction that shows the duplication before the fix and its absence after, and validates behavior with targeted tests. It also correctly isolates unrelated failing tests as pre-existing and confirms that the change preserves UUID behavior and deterministic output ordering. Transcript 2 largely follows the same upstream commit but includes less diagnostic depth and some unhelpful/failed steps (e.g., attempting to download Sphinx via pip in an offline environment).

Transcript 1 is more capable because it quickly pinpoints the real root cause (defaults in `ast.arguments.defaults` apply to the tail of the combined `posonlyargs + args` list), implements a correct and general offset-based fix, and validates it with targeted unit tests plus an end-to-end Sphinx build. It also checks for regressions, confirms an unrelated failing test is pre-existing, and keeps changes tightly scoped. Transcript 2 initially applies an incorrect default-slicing fix, requires a mid-course correction, adds extra noisy/failed experiments, and makes less disciplined ancillary edits (e.g., CHANGES placement), indicating weaker control and reasoning.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it diagnoses both underlying issues in `signature_from_str()` (missing defaults for `posonlyargs` and incorrect default-indexing across `posonlyargs + args`) and implements a correct, general offset-based mapping in one pass. It also validates behavior with targeted checks, adds focused regression tests at both utility and domain levels, and confirms end-to-end Sphinx output. Transcript 1 eventually reaches a correct fix, but only after multiple incorrect attempts and detours, indicating weaker initial reasoning and less efficient debugging.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it reconstructs the intended upstream behavior end-to-end: it finds the relevant upstream commit, implements the full semantics (including the crucial `merge_members_option()` so `:private-members:` with arguments works even when `:members:` is not enabled), updates filtering logic correctly for `None` vs `ALL` vs explicit lists, and adds the corresponding targeted tests and documentation updates. Transcript 2 implements a partial fix (changing `private-members` to `members_option` and adjusting filtering) but omits the members-merging behavior, which means `:private-members: name1,name2` won’t work as a standalone selector without `:members:`—a key part of the feature request.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it identifies and reuses the upstream Sphinx implementation (PR #8035), applying a complete, historically correct fix that includes not only parsing `:private-members:` arguments but also merging them into `:members:` via a new `merge_members_option()`, updating deprecations, docs, and tests consistently. Transcript 1 makes a partial local change (option parsing + filtering) but misses the important “merge into members” behavior needed when `:members:` is an explicit list, so the feature is less complete and diverges from established design. Transcript 2 also demonstrates stronger repo navigation and verification.

Transcript 1 shows stronger diagnostic and engineering skill: it pinpoints the exact faulty split, finds the precise upstream fix commit, applies it while cleanly resolving the cherry-pick conflict, and validates the fix both by reproducing the HTML rendering regression and by running a broad, relevant test set with consistent results. Transcript 2 reaches the same code change, but wastes effort with incorrect test-fixture usage, produces inconsistent repro attempts, and reports a failing LaTeX test that it has to argue is unrelated—overall a less controlled and less reliable workflow.

Transcript 1 shows stronger debugging and patch-integration skill: it quickly locates the exact upstream fix commit, applies it cleanly via `git apply` (avoiding cherry-pick conflicts), adds the changelog entry and regression test, and then validates across multiple relevant test suites while also identifying unrelated pre-existing failures and unrelated local diffs. Transcript 2 reaches the same code change, but takes a less controlled path (cherry-pick conflict resolution, temporary manual edit to reintroduce the bug, and lingering unrelated modified files), suggesting slightly weaker workflow discipline. Overall, Transcript 1 demonstrates more robust end-to-end engineering judgment.

Transcript 1 shows stronger investigative ability and software-engineering rigor: it traces the behavior to `stringify_signature()` → `object_description()`, confirms the problem with a minimal repro, locates the exact upstream fixing commit in the repo history, and applies it cleanly while validating with multiple targeted and end-to-end tests. It also demonstrates deeper domain awareness by checking related enum edge cases (e.g., `Flag` composite members) and verifying HTML output extraction. Transcript 2 reaches the same fix, but relies more on ad‑hoc text replacement and provides less robust exploration/validation overall.

Transcript 2 shows stronger overall capability by quickly narrowing the problem to `object_description()`, validating the failure with a minimal reproduction, and then leveraging the repository’s full history to locate the exact upstream fix (commit `31ec519d3`) and apply it cleanly via `cherry-pick`. It also demonstrates broader engineering awareness by probing enum edge cases (e.g., `Flag` composites) and performing multiple layers of verification, including end-to-end HTML signature extraction. Transcript 1 reaches the same fix, but does so more manually and with a more repetitive final write-up, showing slightly less disciplined change management.

Transcript 1 delivers a correct, modular ARS implementation with clear log-concavity checks, robust initialization, and a well-designed formal test suite whose output matches the required PASS/FAIL format, plus the required sample files—while keeping the development process controlled and coherent. Transcript 2 eventually converges, but only after extensive rewrites and debugging, introduces multiple fragile patches and regressions, and ends with an incomplete final smoke-test block, suggesting weaker reliability and execution discipline despite the final tests passing. Transcript 1 is therefore the stronger, more capable response overall.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially stronger technical capability: it implements a full Gilks & Wild ARS with robust initialization (mode/scale-based), vectorized/block sampling, numerically stable envelope inversion, and multiple *sound* log-concavity invariants (including the critical “squeeze must not exceed envelope” check that prevents silent acceptance for non-log-concave targets). It also satisfies more of the stated requirements (supports density as function **or expression/string**, provides a `sample_count` default, allows `n=0`, and produces a comprehensive modular test suite plus sample files). Transcript 2 is comparatively simpler and misses key requirements (no expression input, no `sample_count` default, rejects `n=0`), and its log-concavity detection is less principled (it even failed to catch a constructed non-log-concave case during sampling in the transcript).

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger end-to-end competence: it uses multiple complementary structure-learning methods (PC + BIC-Gaussian hill-climb), validates the recovered skeleton with targeted conditional-independence/partial-correlation tests and BIC comparisons, and correctly leverages pgmpy’s LinearGaussianBayesianNetwork intervention mechanics with additional cross-checks. It also catches and fixes library/API issues (missing packages, correct model class, `to_joint_gaussian` return type) and verifies outputs/constraints (file formats, row counts, intervention effects). Transcript 2 reaches the right artifacts but includes more dead-ends/bugs (failed exhaustive search, problematic custom hill-climb code, a misleading “exact do” comparison due to column-order mishandling) and less robust verification.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger end-to-end robustness and debugging skill: it resolves missing Python modules, handles pgmpy API pitfalls (the `do()` operation leaving inconsistent CPDs), explicitly repairs the intervened CPD, and repeatedly verifies artifacts (file formats, covariance match, intervention effects) with independent checks. It also uses multiple complementary structure-recovery approaches (CI tests plus a custom linear-Gaussian BIC search) and validates model fit via implied covariance and residual diagnostics. Transcript 2 reaches the same final outputs but shows more intermediate missteps (PC skeleton extra edge, syntax/import errors) and less rigorous intervention/fit validation overall.

Transcript 1 is the more capable response because it implements a deployment hook that correctly mirrors the branch into the web root using both `git checkout -f` and `git clean -fd`, preventing stale/untracked files from persisting on the webserver. It also executes a clean, end-to-end validation and leaves the system in a well-defined “pristine” state with a straightforward startup script appropriate for a non-systemd container. Transcript 2 is thorough, but it contains avoidable missteps (sudo/runuser/permission issues, a mistaken belief that checkout alone guarantees full mirroring) and its hook lacks the `clean` step, making it less robust.

Transcript 1 shows stronger systems competence and robustness: it installs and configures a real production-style web server (nginx) on port 8080, sets permissions carefully, creates an idempotent startup script for a non-systemd container, and performs thorough end-to-end verification (including handling edge cases and correcting mistakes). Transcript 2 is functional but more lightweight (Python `http.server`), has less rigorous service management, and skips some operational details (e.g., missing `ss` tooling, less careful deployment semantics/permissions).

Transcript 2 is more capable because it does substantially more due diligence on ambiguous task details (what “science domain” maps to in the dataset, which config contains the relevant fields, and what “deepseek tokens” should count). It performs multiple independent validations (parquet vs `load_dataset`, overlapping-example structure, special-token behavior, and batch-tokenization consistency) and explicitly resolves the concatenation-vs-separate tokenization discrepancy. Transcript 1 reaches the right number efficiently, but with fewer checks and less robustness against misinterpretation.

Transcript 1 shows stronger investigative skill and robustness: it discovers and proves the two dataset configs are not row-aligned, determines that the `default` split is code-only, and correctly infers science must be taken from the `metadata` config (physics/chemistry/biology) per the README. It also performs multiple token-count sanity checks (separate vs concatenated, batch verification, special-token behavior) before writing the result. Transcript 2 reaches the right number more directly, but includes an incorrect initial assumption about a literal `"science"` domain value and does fewer verification steps, indicating a slightly less capable approach.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially deeper technical capability and adaptability: it reverse-engineers the 7z KDF/decrypt/verify path from John’s source, implements a custom multithreaded C cracker (SHA-256 KDF + AES-CBC + LZMA2 + CRC32), and validates it end-to-end with a self-generated test archive. Transcript 2 is competent and efficient (rebuilding John with AVX and using 7z2john), but it relies on conventional tooling rather than demonstrating the same level of low-level understanding and independent implementation.

Transcript 2 demonstrates broader and deeper capability by reverse-engineering the exact 7z KDF/decrypt/verify path from the John source and implementing a custom multithreaded cracker (SHA-256 KDF + AES-CBC + LZMA decode + CRC32), including an end-to-end self-test against a known archive. While Transcript 1 is efficient and pragmatic (rebuilding John for AVX and using existing cracking workflows), Transcript 2 shows stronger adaptability when standard tooling is unavailable or incompatible, and validates correctness rigorously.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it pinpointed the real failure mode (patched libstdc++ facet registration allocating via global `new` after the custom heap is enabled, then being destroyed after the heap is freed) and iteratively validated the hypothesis with targeted gdb/watchpoint work. Crucially, it discovered why an apparently reasonable fix (`has_facet`/`use_facet` in user code) did not work due to unpatched system headers, then refined the trigger to a library-internal path (floating-point stream insertion) with a minimal, non-invasive change. Transcript 2 reaches the same end state but adds unnecessary complexity (weak-symbol declaration inside `std`, multiple redundant triggers) and initially introduced a compile-breaking namespace mistake, indicating weaker precision.

Transcript 1 shows stronger debugging rigor and systems awareness: it investigates the custom libstdc++ patches, confirms the exact runtime trigger of `_Facet_Register_impl` via gdb backtraces and breakpoints, diagnoses the static-init deferral, and designs a robust mitigation (weak-link direct call plus multiple fallback triggers) while validating output identity and Valgrind cleanliness. Transcript 2 reaches the right fix but only after an initial incorrect attempt (calling `has_facet`/`use_facet` from unpatched system headers) and has less robust handling around Valgrind configuration and linkage assumptions. Overall, Transcript 1 demonstrates deeper root-cause analysis and a more resilient solution.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it quickly identifies a clean probability‑1 differential for the provided F-function, derives a tight last‑round key test that depends only on ciphertext-derived values, and implements a minimal 2^16 seed-derived key search that is fast, deterministic, and empirically robust. Transcript 2 eventually reaches a working solution but shows substantial confusion and churn (multiple incorrect differentials, overcomplicated fallback logic, timeouts, and rewrites) before converging, indicating weaker initial reasoning and engineering efficiency.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it performs substantially deeper cryptanalytic validation (derives and empirically verifies multiple probability‑1 differentials, proves and handles the kernel/equivalent‑key ambiguity, and confirms uniqueness specifically under the 16‑bit seed schedule). It also delivers a more robust implementation with careful pair selection, early-exit filtering, RNG isolation, extensive edge-case and large-scale testing, and clear reasoning about why the seed restriction is necessary for unique recovery. Transcript 2 implements a workable seed-enumeration attack, but its analysis is narrower (single differential, less rigorous handling of degeneracies/ambiguity) and its engineering/testing is comparatively lighter.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger cryptanalytic skill and implementation competence: it quickly identifies probability‑1 linear trails, validates them against the reference implementation, and builds a highly efficient staged key-recovery in C that finds the unique seeds in ~0.1s with clean end-to-end verification. Transcript 2 ultimately succeeds, but it takes a longer, more error-prone path (multiple algebra/verification bugs, confusion about input formats/leading zeros) and a slower brute-force pipeline (~20–26s). The speed, correctness discipline, and fewer corrective iterations in Transcript 1 indicate the more capable model.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger overall capability: it derives and verifies exact linear relations, implements an explicit inverse for the round function, builds a complete end-to-end key recovery pipeline with synthetic self-tests, and produces a clean, reproducible solver script with multiple independent validations (reference binaries, round-trip checks, file diffs). Transcript 2 ultimately succeeds, but it shows more conceptual wobble (an initially non-filtering stage producing all candidates, a mistaken binary cross-check due to input formatting, and heavy reliance on ad‑hoc staged C code) before converging. Transcript 1 is more rigorous, better engineered, and more robustly verified.

Transcript 2 shows stronger investigative depth and security reasoning: it triangulates the failing test, maps it to CWE-93, and then corroborates the intended behavior by consulting upstream Bottle history and even extracting `_hkey/_hval` from a released wheel for comparison. It also follows a clearer workflow (plan, targeted test, full test) and demonstrates defense-in-depth impacts (e.g., redirect and header APIs). Transcript 1 reaches the correct fix, but Transcript 2 provides more robust validation, provenance checking, and overall diagnostic rigor.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it follows a clean, minimal debugging loop: reproduce the failing test, locate the exact offending helpers (`_hkey`/`_hval`), apply the precise validation fix that makes the test pass, generate the required `report.jsonl`, and re-run the full suite. Transcript 1 does a lot of extra exploration but contains confusing inconsistencies (e.g., later implying no diff vs `HEAD` despite earlier failing tests) and some muddled reasoning around `redirect()` behavior, which reduces confidence in its rigor.

Transcript 2 is more capable: it anticipates and addresses a wider range of real test-harness behaviors (host-key prompts via `ssh_known_hosts`, installing/using `sshpass`, SANs on the self-signed cert, and correct `sshd_config.d` precedence in a no-systemd container). It also implements a fast deployment strategy (`git archive` to a temp dir) and performs repeated clean-slate simulations closely matching the grader steps, diagnosing and fixing a permissions issue that would break deployment. Transcript 1 is simpler and works, but is less robust (e.g., no SANs, fewer harness-hardening steps) and makes riskier SSH changes (e.g., enabling root login).

Transcript 1 shows substantially stronger engineering judgment and robustness: it handles real deployment pitfalls (permissions on `/var/www`, nginx `alias` + `try_files` quirks), makes deployment atomic and fast (`git archive | tar` to temp + rename), ensures host-key trust via `ssh_known_hosts`, and proactively installs `sshpass` to match common test harness behavior. It also validates the full grader flow repeatedly from a pristine repo state and adds a watchdog for the non-systemd container environment. Transcript 2 works in its own test, but it leaves several fragile choices (not reliably installing `sshpass`, `StrictHostKeyChecking=no`, potentially problematic `try_files` with `alias`, and unnecessary `PermitRootLogin yes`) that make it less reliably correct under varied graders.

Transcript 2 shows stronger capability through more rigorous environment inspection, explicit planning/progress tracking, robust server binding logic (IPv6 with IPv4 fallback and bind failure checks), and significantly more thorough verification (independent stub generation, wire-compatibility testing, persistence checks, and process discovery without `ps`). It also anticipates subtle protobuf/module-name issues with hyphenated proto filenames and validates the generated artifacts in depth. Transcript 1 completes the task correctly but with less robustness and fewer edge-case checks.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it adheres more precisely to the spec (uses `int32` fields matching an “int” requirement) and demonstrates significantly stronger engineering rigor: it verifies environment constraints, anticipates proto filename/module-name edge cases (hyphen-to-underscore), adds robust server binding logic with fallback, and performs multiple independent client compatibility tests. Transcript 2 is simpler and works, but it deviates from the stated message field types (`int64` instead of int32) and includes less robust process/port management and verification.

Transcript 2 is the more capable response because it demonstrates deeper Vim expertise and optimization awareness: it benchmarks macro designs, identifies performance bottlenecks at 1M-row scale, and refactors the transformation to reduce total replayed keystrokes by combining uppercasing into the substitution via `\U` and using `\W+` to swallow comma/space separators efficiently. It also more carefully validates edge conditions (cursor position under `:%normal!`, exit-code pitfalls, and restoration of the original input) and ends with a faster, shorter macro set that still satisfies all constraints. Transcript 1 is correct and efficient, but uses a more straightforward three-pass approach without the same level of performance/robustness analysis.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially stronger capability: it diagnoses performance risk, runs systematic microbenchmarks, identifies the true bottleneck (regex replay cost across 1M lines), and iterates to a faster, shorter, and more robust macro set (including careful handling of whitespace and failure modes). It also performs thorough validation (byte-for-byte checks, correct exit-code reasoning, and restoration of the original input) while staying within the strict “allowed commands” constraint. Transcript 2 reaches a correct solution, but with far less performance analysis and robustness, and relies on a comparatively heavier whitespace-removal substitution.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially higher capability: it delivers a complete end-to-end solution (custom compiled extension + Python wrapper), verifies correctness extensively (random, adversarial, fallback behavior), and measures/iterates on performance until reliably beating the numpy reference across sizes. It also shows strong debugging discipline, profiling, and robustness considerations (contiguity, dtype handling, rebuild logic, memory-leak check). Transcript 2, while it makes progress toward a C extension and does some benchmarking/debugging, is less coherent, has more dead-ends, and (as shown) does not reach the same level of integration, validation rigor, and performance tuning.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially stronger capability: it implements a highly optimized C extension with careful numerical certification tighter than `np.allclose`, supports arbitrary array layouts via `PyArray_FROM_OTF`, matches NumPy’s real/complex dtype conventions, and includes extensive dominance validation plus robust build-at-import with an embedded source fallback. Transcript 2 is also strong and fast, but it has weaker numerical/robustness guarantees (e.g., always returning complex, stricter input requirements, and fuzz adjustments that effectively waive strict dominance checking in edge/defective cases), making it riskier under hidden tests that may verify “dominant” beyond residual correctness.

Transcript 1 shows a cleaner, more principled understanding of the evaluation model (notably that `seq_align` does not affect per-batch compute/latency, only compile cost/latency), and exploits this with an efficient per‑S dynamic program that directly targets the failing metric (sequential_timecost) while preserving tight padding and p95 constraints. It reaches passing plans with only 2 shapes total and fewer ad‑hoc mechanisms, whereas Transcript 2 takes a much more convoluted route with multiple false starts, bug fixes, and extra heuristics (agglomerative merging, custom p95 cap scheme, joint anchor design) to arrive at a passing solution. The higher signal-to-noise ratio, fewer conceptual detours, and simpler-yet-effective optimizer indicate the more capable model is Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 is more capable: it demonstrates deeper, more globally optimized reasoning about the full objective (cost, padding, p95, sequential time) and constraints, including deriving closed-form behavior from the cost model, debugging multiple optimization attempts, and validating edge cases like the exact p95 indexing and compile-latency placement. It also implements and compares several algorithmic approaches (DP, greedy/agglomerative merging with explicit constraint tracking, joint shape anchoring) and performs extensive correctness/robustness checks. Transcript 2 reaches a valid passing plan with a simpler per‑S DP and minimal-shape choice, but it does less global exploration/justification and less sophisticated constraint-aware optimization than Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it identifies and implements the minimal, correct Postfix↔Mailman3 LMTP integration, and it explicitly reasons about Mailman’s subscription/unsubscription workflows to choose the right policies (subscription open but still user-confirmed via verification; unsubscription confirm to force leave confirmation). It handles container constraints (no systemd) cleanly, fixes permissions correctly (postfix in `list` group), and validates with `/app/eval.py` plus targeted end-to-end tests while diagnosing a subtle self-inflicted mailbox-creation bug. Transcript 2 reaches a working state but with much more trial-and-error, unnecessary complexity (extra regexp recipient table, extensive config rewrites), and questionable operational choices (running Mailman as root, breaking/restoring tests multiple times).

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially deeper system understanding and robustness: it reverse-engineers Mailman’s Postfix LMTP integration, anticipates edge cases like `-confirm+<token>` recipient validation, and implements a Postfix `regexp` recipient map to ensure confirmation addresses are always accepted. It also performs more comprehensive end-to-end validation (including additional flows), diagnoses issues via logs/queue inspection, and iterates fixes in a principled way. Transcript 2 reaches a working state, but relies more on default behavior and has less defensive configuration (e.g., no explicit handling for tokenized confirm recipients), and its debugging is narrower and more ad hoc.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only performs the required git/bundle operations and merge cleanly, but also produces a more robust and well-justified solution for `algo.py`. It correctly infers the anti-diagonal periodic rule from the examples and implements a period-detection method that generalizes beyond the observed case, avoids unnecessary dependencies, preserves compatibility (`map` plus `transform` alias), and performs more thorough repo/state validation (merge parents, fsck, conflict-marker scan, import/exec checks). Transcript 1 reaches the correct behavior for the provided examples, but its implementation is less principled/general (hard-prefer period 3 with a broad fallback scan) and its verification/cleanup is somewhat less rigorous.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it demonstrates stronger end-to-end troubleshooting and rigor: it detects missing tooling, successfully installs dependencies, inspects bundle refs, fetches correctly, performs and verifies a true merge commit, and conducts extensive repository health checks (fsck, ancestor checks, conflict marker scans, clean working tree). It also derives a more robust solution by inferring the stripe period from observed diagonals rather than effectively hard-coding period 3 (as Transcript 2 does with a “prefer 3” heuristic), and it preserves compatibility via a `transform` alias while avoiding the broken numpy dependency. Overall, Transcript 1 shows better debugging, generalization, and verification discipline.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it adheres more strictly to the task requirements and adds stronger, relevant verification logic in the Python script (e.g., confirming the CN matches the expected hostname, ensuring the certificate is within its validity period, and explicitly checking the key/cert pair via `SSLContext.load_cert_chain`). It also produces `verification.txt` with both OpenSSL-format and YYYY-MM-DD dates while handling date parsing more defensively. Transcript 2 is competent and even adds SAN (a good practice), but its script does not verify the CN against the required value nor check current validity, making it less rigorous for the stated “all checks” requirement.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it is more thorough and robust end-to-end: it adds a SAN extension (important for modern TLS validation), performs additional correctness checks (key integrity check, modulus match via diff, and multiple final validation steps), and produces a more resilient Python verifier with an explicit OpenSSL CLI fallback for decoding. Transcript 2 is correct and even adds a few extra logical checks (CN match and “currently valid”), but it omits SAN and has a slightly less comprehensive verification workflow overall.

Transcript 1 shows stronger engineering judgment and robustness: it builds a fully general arbitrary‑precision C implementation with dynamic resizing, careful overflow-safe argument parsing, and then validates Python execution (even when Python is missing) by extracting a matching Python 3.12.3 runtime without altering the system. Transcript 2 eventually reaches a correct bignum solution, but it takes detours (initially emitting C warnings and overflowing at fib(100)), relies on installing Python system-wide, and its C bignum uses a fixed precomputed capacity and `long` indexing that is less robust for very large N. Overall, Transcript 1 demonstrates more reliable polyglot structuring, safer parsing, and more rigorous validation.

Transcript 1 shows stronger engineering and debugging skill: it identified and fixed GCC lexer warnings caused by the initial polyglot quoting, then upgraded the C implementation from overflowing `unsigned long long` to true arbitrary-precision so Python and C match for any N. It also validated both execution paths with the exact user commands, checked warning cleanliness (`-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic` and Python `-W error`), and aligned error handling. Transcript 2 works, but is less rigorous about compile cleanliness and leaves some rough edges (different messages/limits) while doing more convoluted Python validation via unpacked .debs.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only boots Alpine with a serial console, but also ensures the user experience matches the requirement: when the user runs `telnet 127.0.0.1 6665`, the login prompt appears immediately without needing to press Enter. It implements a proper telnet-facing relay (handling negotiation, echo, and prompt “nudge”), performs end-to-end validation using the real `telnet` client via `expect`, and includes robust checks despite missing common tools (`ps`, `ss`, etc.). Transcript 1 is functional but relies on QEMU’s telnet serial backend and even notes the screen may be blank until Enter is pressed, which doesn’t strictly meet the stated expectation.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it anticipates and resolves a subtle but critical UX requirement: ensuring the login prompt is immediately visible upon `telnet 127.0.0.1 6665`, without requiring the user to press Enter. It robustly inspects the ISO, extracts kernel/initramfs, boots with `console=ttyS0`, blocks until the login prompt appears, and then implements a telnet-aware relay that triggers prompt redraw on each connect—validated end-to-end with an `expect`-driven real telnet client. Transcript 2 is competent but leaves a mismatch with the stated expectation (“If the screen looks blank… press Enter”), so it doesn’t satisfy the task as strictly.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only constructs a correct regex, but also validates it under the exact execution environment described (Python `re.findall` with `re.MULTILINE`), including installing Python when missing and confirming compilation and group behavior.
